evidence.title: Do No Harm? Hallucination and Actor-Level Abuse in Web-Deployed Medical Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Adequacy of privacy disclosures among Action-enabled MedGPTs
evidence.effect: 57.06% of Action-enabled models lack adequate privacy disclosures.
evidence.quote: Our results show that 25-30% of MedGPTs exhibit low factual accuracy, with bottom- and middle-tier models at highest risk; 33.6-54.3% violate operational thresholds, and 57.06% of Action-enabled models lack adequate privacy disclosures.
evidence.sample_unit: MedGPTs (custom medical GPTs, stratified sample from 6,233)

commentary.bottom_line: Thirteen sources endorse telling patients through the Notice of Privacy Practices and published notices how AI uses their data, but no study tests whether such notices improve patient awareness or reduce privacy harm. The one related study documents disclosure gaps in custom medical GPTs and does not evaluate the recommended practice.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so the certainty rating is no direct evidence. The single hazard study is an automated benchmark of custom medical GPTs rather than health system notices, and it is indirect to the question. The endorsements come mostly from commentaries and frameworks, which reflect expert agreement rather than measured effects on patients.

An automated review sampled 1,500 of 6,233 custom medical GPTs and found that 57.06% of the Action-enabled models lacked adequate privacy disclosures. This suggests that people may use some AI tools without knowing how their data are handled. The study does not show whether an updated notice would prevent that exposure.

The CHAI playbook points out that the HIPAA Privacy Rule already requires covered providers and health plans to distribute a notice explaining privacy rights and practices. Adding AI content to that notice would build on an existing legal duty. No study reports whether regulators or patients find such AI language adequate or understandable.

The benchmark found that 57.06% of Action-enabled models in a sample of custom medical GPTs lacked adequate privacy disclosures, which suggests that some patients may not be able to learn how AI tools use their information. No study has measured whether a revised notice gives patients usable knowledge of their rights or a way to reach a person with questions.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare AI-specific language in the Notice of Privacy Practices and public web notices against the standard notice and measure patient comprehension, trust, opt-out use, and complaint rates. They should also measure how many patients read these notices at all.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, and the hazard study did not report patient populations, so there is no evidence for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Notices written only in English or at high reading levels may reach these groups less well, but no study has tested this.
